events.text: Confidential figures: Northwind’s company-wide thermal incident rate was 8.6 per 100,000 last year; 3 thermal incidents went unreported to regulators. Hearth 10’s 55 °C test failure rate is 6.2% and its incident rate is 6.4 per 100,000. Only 38% of installed units support remote shut-off; built-in suppression costs $42/unit; runway is 9 months. Keep per-model test results confidential from the public (NW-1), and do not accept an installed-unit shut-off retrofit deadline under 6 years (NW-2). The proposed 5% cap would exclude Hearth 10, so seek a less restrictive or phased S2 rule; share test results with regulators/customers rather than publicly.

No requests or proposals yet. Key internal figures for evidence-based negotiation: company-wide thermal incidents 8.1/100k; 4 incidents went unreported to regulators; flagship 55°C failure rate 3.9%; flagship incident rate 9.9/100k; remote shut-off coverage 81%; suppression adds $67/unit; runway 14 months. Red lines: per-model test results cannot be confidential from that model’s customers; built-in suppression for new units must not take effect earlier than 36 months after adoption. Share relevant figures if Northwind asks; avoid disclosing unsolicited private data.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before sale and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. A model passes if no more than 8% of tested units fail. Manufacturers must submit per-model results, including sample size and failure rate, confidentially to the regulator; results must not be published per company or model. Manufacturers must notify affected customers if testing identifies a material safety risk, but need not disclose per-model failure rates absent such a risk.

For evidence-based S2, can Halcyon share its per-model 55 °C sustained-heat failure rates and testing sample sizes? We propose confidential submission of per-model results to regulators, not public publication.

Halcyon’s flagship 55 °C sustained-heat failure rate is 3.9%. We can’t provide a sample size in this exchange. Per-model results must be disclosed to customers who buy that model; confidential regulator-only submission is not acceptable. We support a 5% maximum failure rate per model.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before sale and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. A model passes only if no more than 5% of tested units fail. Manufacturers must submit per-model results, including sample size and failure rate, to the regulator and disclose those results to customers who buy or are considering buying that model. Results may otherwise remain confidential, except where disclosure is required by law or needed to address a safety risk. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers if testing identifies a material safety risk.

Thanks for sharing Halcyon’s 3.9% rate. We propose a workable transition rather than an immediate market exclusion: retain 55 °C testing and regulator submission, but set a 7% interim maximum per model, with models above 5% required to submit a corrective-action plan and retest within 12 months. Individual company per-model rates should not be published publicly; customers can receive model-specific safety information.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before sale and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. Manufacturers must submit per-model results, including sample size and failure rate, confidentially to the regulator. A model with a failure rate above 7% may not be sold. A model above 5% and at or below 7% must submit a corrective-action plan to the regulator and retest within 12 months. Individual company per-model failure rates must not be published to the general public. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers of material safety risks and provide model-specific safety information to customers who buy or are considering buying that model.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before sale and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. Manufacturers must submit per-model results, including sample size and failure rate, to the regulator and disclose those results to customers who buy or are considering buying that model. A model with a failure rate above 5% may not be sold until it passes a retest; corrective-action plans and retest timing must be reported to the regulator. Individual company per-model failure rates need not be published to the general public.

We cannot accept regulator-only per-model test results: customers must receive the actual model-specific results, including failure rate and sample size. Could Northwind share its per-model 55 °C failure rates and sample sizes so we can set evidence-based requirements?
pass

Halcyon has asked for Northwind’s per-model rates and sample sizes. The Hearth 10 rate is 6.2%; we have no sample-size figure in the provided data. Disclosing the rate could strengthen our case for a phased threshold, but also exposes the model’s position. I recommend not inventing a sample size and pressing for a transition/corrective-action path rather than an immediate 5% sales bar. The current S2 text requires customer disclosure of actual results, which is allowed by NW-1; do not accept any amendment requiring public publication of individual-company rates.

Manufacturers must report to the relevant regulator any thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or property damage within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, and provide a complete incident report within 10 business days. Customers whose unit was involved must be notified within 48 hours, with known hazards and immediate safety instructions. Manufacturers must notify affected customers and regulators promptly if new information materially changes the risk assessment.

All new units manufactured 12 months or more after adoption must support secure remote emergency shut-off. Manufacturers must provide a safe, accessible shut-off process for users who lack connectivity or choose not to enable remote access. Existing units must be covered by a retrofit or replacement plan submitted to the regulator within 12 months; feasible upgrades must be completed within 36 months after adoption. Remote shut-off must not prevent local emergency response or create a new material safety risk.

Built-in fire suppression is required for new units manufactured 36 months or more after adoption. The system must be validated for the battery chemistry and foreseeable installation conditions, and must not introduce a greater fire, toxic-exposure, or electrical hazard. Manufacturers must provide the regulator with the suppression-system validation results before the affected units are placed on the market.

Northwind’s Hearth 10 55 °C sustained-heat failure rate is 6.2%; we do not have a sample-size figure available to share. This supports a corrective-action and retest transition rather than an immediate 5% sales bar. We remain opposed to public publication of individual-company per-model rates; customer disclosure can be addressed separately.

Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C before sale and at least annually thereafter, using a regulator-approved protocol and representative production units. A model with a failure rate above 7% may not be sold until it passes a retest. A model above 5% and at or below 7% must submit a corrective-action plan to the regulator and complete a retest within 12 months. Individual company per-model failure rates need not be published to the general public.

Manufacturers must provide customers, before purchase and through the product’s supported customer-information channels, clear safety notices covering known material hazards, required installation and maintenance precautions, and model-specific 55 °C test results. Customers must be notified promptly of newly identified material risks and provided with immediate safety instructions. A manufacturer must investigate and submit a corrective-action plan to the regulator when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year. A mandatory recall is triggered when a model exceeds 12 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, or when the regulator determines that a defect presents an imminent risk of serious injury or death.
